name: Brian Levack
specialization: Comparative prosecution statistics, legal history of witch trials, cumulative concept of witchcraft

major_works.title: The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe
major_works.significance: Standard textbook synthesis of European witch-hunting with comprehensive prosecution statistics and multi-causal analysis

major_works.title: Witch-Hunting in Scotland: Law, Politics and Religion
major_works.significance: Detailed study of Scottish prosecutions integrating legal and political factors

major_works.title: The Devil Within: Possession and Exorcism in the Christian West
major_works.significance: Comparative study of demonic possession extending Levack's legal-religious framework

core_argument: The European witch-hunt was driven by the convergence of a cumulative demonological concept of witchcraft (sabbath, Devil's pact, maleficium combined) and specific legal changes — particularly the adoption of Roman-canon inquisitorial procedure with judicial torture — that made prosecution and chain-reaction panics possible. No single cause suffices; a multi-causal model is required.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Trial records across multiple European jurisdictions, legal codes, ecclesiastical procedure manuals
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Prosecution rates, legal procedures, regional variation in outcomes
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Quantitative statistical analysis of prosecutions; comparative legal-institutional analysis
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Macro-structural: legal and institutional factors driving aggregate prosecution patterns

key_contributions.claim: Witch trials required the coalescence of maleficium, Devil's pact, and sabbath attendance into a single crime; without this cumulative concept, prosecution chains could not develop
key_contributions.implication: The intellectual history of demonological synthesis directly enabled mass prosecution

key_contributions.claim: Adoption of torture-permitted Roman-canon procedure in secular courts allowed confessions to name accomplices, creating chain reactions
key_contributions.implication: Institutional legal reform (not just belief) was a proximate cause of large-scale hunts

key_contributions.claim: Approximately 110,000 tried and 60,000 executed across Europe; highest rates in German territories, Scotland, and Switzerland
key_contributions.implication: Empirical baseline that contextualizes regional studies and challenges exaggerated popular estimates

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Legal history, comparative European history, institutional analysis
criticisms: Multi-causal framework sometimes criticized as too eclectic or insufficiently explanatory
Statistics debated by regional specialists who find local patterns do not match aggregate model
Less attention to individual agency and micro-level dynamics than microhistorians prefer

historiographical_significance: Levack's synthesis is the standard reference work for the European witch-hunt in academic and pedagogical contexts. His insistence on multi-causality and rigorous prosecution statistics set the baseline for all subsequent comparative work. The multiple revised editions of his textbook reflect sustained engagement with new regional scholarship.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
